fields.lessonRecap: Leadership is recorded; wider participation needs further evidence. Being a resident or being affected does not automatically mean joining. fields.title: A Leader Was Not the Whole Community
fields.content:
A leader can guide an action, but a movement involves more than one biography. A leader summary may name an organizer without naming everyone who took part. It does not establish every participants wishes or make all residents participants. Ask which role and action the source actually records.

Compare fictional cards for a leader summary, a participant list and an affected household. The first helps identify leadership. The second concerns recorded participation. The third concerns an experience that might not involve joining. These cards are teaching models, not surviving registers. One person might have more than one role, while some contributors remain unnamed. Do not invent particular historical jobs or speeches to fill the gaps. A missing name is not proof that no one contributed.

Open the three clues, then choose the explanation they support. Use Explain for help or return to this lesson before targeted practice.

fields.title: Gabriela Silang Continued the Movement
fields.content:
The NHCP Gabriela Silang marker identifies her continuation of the Ilocos uprising after Diego Silangs death in 1763. This keeps a womans recorded leadership visible rather than treating her only as a relationship in someone elses biography. The case also shows that a movement could continue through a change in leadership.

The later marker is not a transcript of meetings or a complete membership record. We use its bounded continuation claim without inventing speeches, exact participant numbers or a universal account of all womens roles. Our sequence guide separates Diego, the leadership change and Gabrielas continuation; it is not a battle plan. Conflict caused harm, but students do not reenact attacks or punishment or gain points for them. Recognizing a named womans action does not mean that only famous leaders mattered or that every participant shared one experience.

Open the three clues, then choose the explanation they support. Use Explain for help or return to this lesson before targeted practice.

fields.title: Spread Was Not Everyone Joining
fields.content:
The Sumuroy marker describes an uprising beginning at Palapag in 1649 and spreading to other places. Spread is a historical claim about a wider reach, not proof that every resident of those places joined. Different local actions and degrees of involvement need their own evidence.

Our fictional source desk compares a place mentioned in an account with a list of named people. A place entry helps locate a reported event; a name entry can support recorded participation. Neither reveals every private motive. Do not use a regional label as a vote by all households, or turn later administrative boundaries into exact historical areas of control. A movement may affect people who never joined. To explain a particular town, seek its dated records and compare the actions described. The desk is not a reconstruction of Sumuroys participant register.

Open the three clues, then choose the explanation they support. Use Explain for help or return to this lesson before targeted practice.

fields.title: Roles and Conditions Could Differ
fields.content:
People in a community could face different resources, responsibilities and pressures. A leader, participant and affected resident did not necessarily have the same options. Historical agency means people could act within conditions, not that everyone had equal power or unlimited freedom.

Compare fictional role cards: one records an organizing action and another records a household affected by events. Identify only what the cards support. Do not assign roles automatically from gender, religion, ancestry or occupation. Nor should a lack of a famous name make a persons experience unimportant. These cards do not invent a real historical family or ask learners to disclose family income or identity. To explain an actual case, keep the person, place, period, action and evidence together. Claims about voluntary participation or pressure require evidence rather than a guess from a label.

Open the three clues, then choose the explanation they support. Use Explain for help or return to this lesson before targeted practice.

fields.title: Build a Participation Portfolio
fields.content:
A participation report should identify who is recorded, what action is described and what remains uncertain. A later marker can commemorate a leader without listing all participants. A movement span can extend beyond its founder. Sources about different places and stages should not be merged into one complete community biography.

CulturEd notes that the Dagohoy movement continued after its founder, while the Gabriela marker records a specific leadership continuation in another case. These examples are not the same event or proof of a shared command. Our fictional portfolio separates leadership evidence, a participation record and an account of affected residents. Match the question to the source, check its date and purpose, and state a limit. Do not invent a universal national program, private conversations or membership where the evidence is incomplete. Later Mission 5 will examine outcomes and significance.

Open the three clues, then choose the explanation they support. Use Explain for help or return to this lesson before targeted practice.

fields.title: Prepare Your Leaders and Communities Report
fields.content:
Review five ideas. A leader was not the whole community. Gabriela Silangs continuation keeps her leadership visible and illustrates a movement changing leaders. Spread did not mean every resident joined. Different roles came with different conditions and pressures. Sources have scope and cannot automatically supply every participants story.

Prepare a fictional report for another Grade 5 learner. Name a person or community, place and period, give evidence of an action and identify a limit. Separate leaders, participants and affected residents. Do not invent member counts, assign roles from gender or ancestry, or make a modern map color prove historical participation. Keep movement stages distinct and do not turn harm into a reward.

The main quiz has five questions and three correct passes. Review linked learning content before practice and a retry if needed. Completing this mission earns its configured reward once, but does not complete Chapter 12. Mission 5 and the chapter challenge are still being prepared.
